title: Ruben Hassid: Why taste is the edge when AI output is average
summary: Ruben explains how he grew a large AI audience by testing tools for himself and sharing only what works. His thesis: AI output is average and commoditized, so taste and a unique vision are what stay valuable. He also argues for building on the side of a job, ignoring money early, and learning AI by playing with one task.

principles.text: Teach what you tested for yourself: publish only when it works and isn't obvious.
principles.quote: I'm still testing stuff to help myself as and as soon as is it is very useful and not obvious something I can actually teach you that is new then it's worth an article or a post.

principles.text: Don't chase money early; escape velocity comes from doing something else exceptionally well.
principles.quote: the more you forget about making money, the more money you make.

principles.text: Build the new thing on top of a job; if you can't handle both, you likely couldn't handle it alone.
principles.quote: you have a job and you do it on top of it and if you cannot handle it then you could probably not handle it just that and trying to make money anyway

principles.text: Generic AI output is average, so your edge is a unique vision and taste.
principles.quote: You really need to ask yourself what is so unique about my vision on doing something.

principles.text: Encode your taste, opinions and boundaries into a reusable file that steers any AI like you.
principles.quote: we created something that is like a genie in a bottle of most of my opinion, most of my tastes.

principles.text: Beat AI decision paralysis: pick one thing, treat it as a game, go deep on it.
principles.quote: pick one thing, do it as a as a game. Go down the rabbit hole. You don't have to master everything.
